title: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning Using PPA and MiniMax Game Theory

C-a.quote: We engineer our approach through the combination of (1) a reputation system to evaluate and track client behavior, (2) an incentive mechanism to reward honest participation and penalize malicious behavior, and (3) game theoretical models with projection pursuit analysis (PPA) to dynamically identify and minimize the impact of malicious clients on the global model.
C-a.locator: Abstract; THREE COMPONENTS EACH WITH THEIR OWN DEFENSE-PURPOSE QUOTATION, as Amendment 3 requires. (1) The kurtosis-based PPA detector: "This property makes kurtosis-based PPA particularly effective for identifying stealthy backdoor behaviors embedded in model updates." (§III), restated as "The kurtosis-based PPA aims to identify extreme nonGaussian deviations that may indicate malicious behavior, rather than capturing normal variance from benign data heterogeneity." (§V). (2) The reputation system: "2) Leverage a reputation mechanism to evaluate client behavior dynamically, rewarding honest clients and penalizing malicious ones, thereby enhancing the robustness of the global model against backdoor attacks." (§I), and the score it computes is "The reputation score for client i at round t is: Ri (t) = αHi (t) + βGi (t) (10) where Hi (t) represents historical behavior, Gi (t) captures gradient variation and α,β are weights such that α + β = 1." (§V). (3) The MiniMax game and its weighting: "The MiniMax game framework dynamically counters attackers, while the reputation system enhances decisionmaking. This multifaceted approach provides a comprehensive solution to mitigating malicious clients in federated learning." (§IV). The stages are sequential within one round, "Algorithm 2 Round-Based Execution of the FedBBA Framework 1: Initialize global model M0 , reputation scores Ri 2: for each federated learning round r in 1 to T do 3: for each client i in 1 to N do 4: Train local model Mi on client’s data 5: Send local model Mi to server 6: end for 7: Calculate PPA score si = PPA(Mi ) 8: Cluster PPA scores using DBSCAN to determine classes 9: for each client i in classes do 10: Compute normalized weights using Equation (17) 11: if classi == 0 then 12: Update reputation score Ri negatively using Equation (14) 13: else 14: Update reputation score Ri positively using Equation (13) 15: end if 16: end for 17: Update global model using Equation (18) 18: Calculate server’s payoff using Equation (21) 19: Calculate attacker’s payoff using Equation (22)" (Algorithm 2): PPA score, then DBSCAN over the PPA scores, then the reputation update, then the weighted global update, then the two payoffs. UNDER THE GRANULARITY RULE the DBSCAN step is not counted separately -- it is a stage in computing the PPA signal, not an independent decision -- and the incentive mechanism's reward and penalty factors are the reputation stage's update rule rather than a fourth mechanism; counting either way leaves C-a at YES.

C-b.quote: By combining PPA anomaly detection with reputation tracking, the system identifies persistent malicious behaviors rather than incidental irregularities.
C-b.locator: §V; the reason for pairing turns on a property of the constituents -- the PPA detector fires on per-round anomaly, the reputation stage accumulates across rounds, and the pair is chosen so that persistence rather than incidence is what gets penalized. This is the DISCRIMINATION kind of reason, and the discriminative burden is stated for the detector on its own as well: "The kurtosis-based PPA aims to identify extreme nonGaussian deviations that may indicate malicious behavior, rather than capturing normal variance from benign data heterogeneity." (§V). The contributions list states the coupling in the same terms, "3) Utilize Projection Pursuit Analysis (PPA) with Kurtosis scores, coupled with a reputation mechanism, to identify possible suspicious client updates and mitigate their impact on the global model by reducing the influence of backdoored contributions." (§I).

C-c.quote: Extensive simulations on the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB) and Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC) datasets demonstrate that FedBBA reduces the backdoor attack success rate to approximately 1.1%–11% across various attack scenarios, significantly outperforming stateof-the-art defenses like RDFL and RoPE, which yielded attack success rates between 23% and 76%, while maintaining high normal task accuracy (∼95%–98%).
C-c.locator: Abstract and §VII; the outcome is the assembled framework's own backdoor attack success rate and normal-task accuracy, against RDFL, RoPE and Vanilla over two datasets and several attack scenarios: "Fig. 4. Backdoor success rate comparison of RDFL, Vanilla, FedBBA, and RoPE across datasets and attack scenarios over 100 communication rounds.". This is the vocabulary C-c was written for -- 89 occurrences of backdoor and 25 of attack success -- and the composed system is what is measured.

C-d.locator: Table II and §VII-B; THE PAPER CALLS IT A SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS AND RUNS IT UNDER ATTACK: "To evaluate the impact of the reputation score’s weighting parameters, we performed a sensitivity analysis on the values of α and β, which represent the contribution of historical behavior and gradient-based anomaly signals, respectively. We constrained α + β = 1 and varied each to assess the effect on both clean-task accuracy and backdoor success rate.". Nine settings of the reputation score's weighting are reported, the attack and dataset are fixed (GTSRB, 100 rounds), the downstream weighting and MiniMax stage are unchanged, and BOTH outcomes are read off the composed system at every setting -- accuracy from 95.4 to 96.9 percent and backdoor success rate from 16 to 45 percent. The paper then draws the design conclusion from it: "As illustrated in Table II, the balanced configuration α = β = 0.5 provides a better trade-off between clean accuracy and backdoor resilience. It achieves one of the highest accuracy values 96.8%, while minimizing the backdoor success rate to just 16%." and "This empirical evidence justifies our choice of equal weights in the reputation calculation." (§VII-B, the two spans separated because a second copy of Table II is interposed mid-sentence in the extracted stream). What varies is the mix of the two signals inside the upstream reputation score; what is held fixed is the aggregation weight of Equation (17) and the equilibrium solution for lambda.

C-e.quote: The MiniMax game framework dynamically counters attackers, while the reputation system enhances decisionmaking. This multifaceted approach provides a comprehensive solution to mitigating malicious clients in federated learning.
C-e.locator: §IV; the claim names each constituent and says what it contributes to the composed result. A measured constituent-level attribution is at §V, "These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PPA for detecting anomalous model updates in federated learning.", supported by the PPA-versus-PCA separation figure, and the sweep supplies a third at §VII-B, "As illustrated in Table II, the balanced configuration α = β = 0.5 provides a better trade-off between clean accuracy and backdoor resilience. It achieves one of the highest accuracy values 96.8%, while minimizing the backdoor success rate to just 16%.".

PRIMARY = NO, AND THE C-d ARM IS THE CLEANEST HYPERPARAMETER-ROUTE INSTANCE IN THE FRAME. Nine settings, an explicit "sensitivity analysis" label, a fixed attack, a fixed downstream stage, and the BACKDOOR SUCCESS RATE reported at every setting. Put beside FedEMA-Distill (2603.04422), coded two rows earlier, it makes the hyperparameter route's two requirements concrete and contrastive: FedEMA sweeps four temperatures with the downstream fixed but with no adversary present, and fails; FedBBA sweeps nine weightings with the downstream fixed and an adversary present, and passes. A5 should present the pair together, because it shows the route's floor is not a technicality -- it separates two papers whose sweeps look identical in shape.

DESIGN = YES AND EVERY CRITERION IS YES, WHICH MAKES THIS ROW THE FRAME'S BEST-EXECUTED NEGATIVE FOR THE PRIMARY QUANTITY. C-a, C-b, C-c, C-d and C-e are all YES; the row falls out of the numerator solely on the negation of C-d, which is exactly what the primary quantity is supposed to do. Together with RKD, LASA and FedSAC it is part of the answer to a reader who suspects the primary rate is an artifact of a criterion nobody could satisfy: several papers do satisfy it, and the ones that do are not the weak ones.

A THIRD DISTINCT KIND OF PAIRING REASON APPEARS IN ONE SENTENCE AND IT IS THE SHARPEST DISCRIMINATION-KIND QUOTATION IN THE FRAME. "By combining PPA anomaly detection with reputation tracking, the system identifies persistent malicious behaviors rather than incidental irregularities" states what each constituent can and cannot separate, and pairs them on that basis. Prior discrimination-kind reasons in the frame were about separating malicious updates from heterogeneous benign ones; this one is about separating malicious PERSISTENCE from benign incidence across rounds, i.e. the pair covers a temporal axis neither constituent covers alone.

RELEVANCE BEYOND THE AUDIT, FLAGGED FOR A3 AND FOR THE BIBLIOGRAPHY. This is an FL backdoor-defense paper built on a MINIMAX GAME between server and attacker, with a saddle-point existence result proved via Sion's theorem: "Theorem 1 (Existence of a Nash Saddle-Point Equilibrium)". It is therefore the closest external neighbour to main.tex's own framing that the audit has turned up, and it should be cited in the related-work section on its own merits, not only as an audit row. Two things to say about it there, both true and both in its favour rather than ours: its game is between the server's detection threshold and the attackers' poisoning intensity, so it is a detection game rather than a design-commitment game, and it does not study what happens when one defense stage is composed with another. That is the distinction main.tex needs to draw, and having a real neighbour to draw it against is stronger than the current related-work section's silence.

EXTRACTION HAZARD, A NEW VARIANT OF LAYOUT INTERRUPTION. The sentence that draws the design conclusion from the sweep is split by a SECOND, COMPLETE COPY OF TABLE II -- header, column labels and all nine rows of numbers -- interposed between "a significantly higher backdoor success" and "rate up to 45%". Previous layout interruptions in the frame were running heads and displayed equations of a line or two; this one inserts several hundred characters of tabular data inside a clause, so a coder assembling a quotation across it would produce a sentence containing a table. The C-d quotation is therefore two spans with the interruption elided, and A5's hazard list gains the variant.
